Digital access to public court records should not depend on an expensive private database. Court records are public because open government requires public scrutiny — access is not a luxury (or a basic function of open government). When a paywall stands between the public and the record, the law may remain formally open while practical access becomes a privilege.

A courthouse archive is more than a pile of documents. It shows how judges exercise power, how parties use the courts, and how legal rules operate in actual disputes (orders, opinions, and filings). What does public access mean if a person can see a record only by paying a company that has copied it? It means the public right exists in theory, but the public cannot reliably use it.

Private databases can provide useful search tools, organization, and alerts. That limited improvement should not be confused with ownership of the underlying public information. A company may build a valuable archive — a vault assembled from records that belong to everyone — but the value of the vault does not transfer the public right to inspect what it contains. The database is a convenience; the record is the civic resource.

The burden falls hardest on people who are not buying information as part of a business. A tenant checking a housing case, a defendant seeking an old filing, a researcher studying local enforcement, or a family member trying to understand a proceeding (even when the underlying case is old) may need only one document. A recurring subscription turns that single need into a toll. A fee that repeats at every step can make ordinary accountability impossible.

The problem also reaches speech and journalism. Reporters, advocates, and members of the public often need to compare filings, identify patterns, or verify what happened in a particular case (including journalists and family members). They cannot perform that work if access is rationed by price. Public discussion then follows the records that a well-funded intermediary chooses to collect, index, and expose. That is a narrowing of the public sphere — not merely a search inconvenience.

A public access system does not have to be perfect to be legitimate. It can require safeguards for sensitive information, reasonable authentication, and technical limits against abuse (for example, a docket entry may need redaction before publication). It can also charge for genuinely special services, such as archival reproduction or unusually intensive processing. But the ordinary act of reading a public filing should remain available without a private subscription. The distinction matters: protection of privacy is a legal design problem, while pricing away access is a political choice.

Supporters of restricted systems may point to the cost of scanning, storage, and maintenance. Those costs are real, but they do not answer the central question. Public institutions already decide what records belong in the public archive, what must be sealed, and what safeguards apply. Handing practical access to a private intermediary does not eliminate those duties; it can make them harder to see. The system may be efficient for paying customers and still fail the people whose right it is supposed to serve.

We should treat court records as public infrastructure, with access designed around public use rather than resale. Legislatures and courts can fund searchable portals, publish clear privacy rules, and require timely digital availability (without requiring a subscription). We can judge each proposed restriction by asking whether it protects a concrete interest or merely creates a market barrier. Public records are public — and the responsible decision-makers should make that principle real before another paywall turns an open courthouse into a closed room.
